nodes.statement: To see this, we start from the estimation bias of the largest and smallest eigenvalues of Sigma_0. Let lambda_max(X) and lambda_min(X) be the largest eigenvalue and the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix X, respectively. Since lambda_max(cdot) is a convex function and lambda_min(cdot) is a concave function over the space of symmetric matrices, then by Jensen's inequality, it holds that lambda_max(Sigma_0)=lambda_max(E_n[widehatSigma]) leq E_n[lambda_max(widehatSigma)]~and~lambda_min(Sigma_0)=lambda_min(E_n[widehatSigma]) geq E_n[lambda_min(widehatSigma)], where E_n denotes the expectation with respect to the n-product measures of the data-generating distribution P and the expectation is taken on widehatSigma. Inequalities in~ reveal that, on average, lambda_max(widehatSigma) overestimates its true counterpart lambda_max(Sigma_0), while lambda_min(widehatSigma) underestimates its true counterpart lambda_min(Sigma_0). The spectral bias occurs not only in the estimation of the largest and smallest eigenvalues but also in the estimation of all other eigenvalues. Let lambda(Sigma_0)triangleq (lambda_1,ldots,lambda_p) be the eigenvalues of Sigma_0, and lambda(widehatSigma)triangleq (widehatlambda_1,ldots,widehatlambda_p) be the eigenvalues of widehatSigma, both in increasing order. In, the authors point out that, on average, lambda(widehatSigma) is more dispersed than lambda(Sigma_0), in the sense that \[ frac1pE_nleft[sum_i=1^p (widehatlambda_i-overlinelambda)^2right] = frac1psum_i=1^p (lambda_i-overlinelambda)^2 + E_n[\|widehatSigma-Sigma_0\|_F^2] > frac1psum_i=1^p (lambda_i-overlinelambda)^2, \] where overlinelambdatriangleq frac1psum_i=1^p lambda_i. The inequality above implies that systematic bias may occur in the estimation of all eigenvalues in a similar manner of~: widehatlambda_i overestimates lambda_i, & when lambda_i is large, \\ widehatlambda_i underestimates lambda_i, & when lambda_i is small.

nodes.name: Spectral divergence
nodes.statement: The divergence D:S^p_+times S^p_+to R_+ satisfies the following structural conditions: [label=(roman*)] item (Orthogonal equivariance) For any X,YinS^p_+ and Vincal O(p), D(X,Y)=D(VXV^top, VYV^top). item (Spectrality) There exists a function d:R_+times R_+to R_+, called the generator of D, such that \[ D(diag(x),diag(y))=sum_i=1^p d(x_i,y_i) forall x,yin R_+^p \] and d(a,b) is twice continuously differentiable in a for every b geq 0. item (Rearrangement property) For any x,yin R_+^p and Vincal O(p) we have \[ D(Vdiag(x^uparrow)V^top, diag(y^uparrow)) geq D(diag(x^uparrow), diag(y^uparrow)). \] If its left side is finite, this inequality becomes an equality if and only if Vdiag(x^uparrow)V^top=diag(x^uparrow).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ass:Spectral-divergence} 
The divergence $D:{\mathbb{S}^p_{+}}\times {\mathbb{S}^p_{+}}\to \mathbb{R}_+$ satisfies the following structural conditions:
        \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item (Orthogonal equivariance) For any $X,Y\in{\mathbb{S}^p_{+}}$ and $V\in{\cal O}(p)$, $D(X,Y)=D(VXV^\top, VYV^\top)$.
    
    \item (Spectrality) There exists a function $d:\mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{R}_+\to \mathbb{R}_+$, called the generator of $D$, such that
    \[
        D(\mathrm{diag}(x),\mathrm{diag}(y))=\sum_{i=1}^p d(x_i,y_i) \quad  \forall x,y\in \mathbb{R}_+^p
    \]
    and $d(a,b)$ is twice continuously differentiable in $a$ for every $b \geq 0$.  
    \item (Rearrangement property) For any $x,y\in \mathbb{R}_+^p$ and $V\in{\cal O}(p)$ we have
    \[
        D(V\mathrm{diag}(x^{\uparrow})V^\top, \mathrm{diag}(y^{\uparrow})) \geq D(\mathrm{diag}(x^{\uparrow}), \mathrm{diag}(y^{\uparrow})).
    \]
    If its left side is finite, this inequality becomes an equality if and only if $V\mathrm{diag}(x^{\uparrow})V^\top=\mathrm{diag}(x^{\uparrow})$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let D be a divergence that satisfies Assumption~. Consider (aI, bI) in dom(D). Then by Assumption~(ii), the domain of d is \[dom(d) = \(a,b)in R_+^2: (aI, bI)in dom(D)\,\] and D(aI, bI) = p times d(a,b). It implies that d inherits non-negativity, continuity, identity of indiscernibles, and convexity from D. \label{remark:minimizer-of-b}
    Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:Spectral-divergence}. Consider $(aI, bI) \in \mathrm{dom}(D)$. Then by Assumption~\ref{ass:Spectral-divergence}(ii), the domain of $d$ is \[\mathrm{dom}(d) = \{(a,b)\in \mathbb{R}_+^2: (aI, bI)\in \mathrm{dom}(D)\},\] and

\label{thm:nonlinear-shrinkage}
    Let Assumptions~\ref{ass:regularity-nominal}-\ref{ass:regularity} hold. Then for any $\tau>0$, $\Sigma^\star(\tau, \rho)$ is continuous in $\rho$ over $(0,  \rho_{\max}]$ and  $\lim_{ \rho\downarrow 0}\Sigma^\star(\tau, \rho)=\widehat\Sigma$, $\Sigma^\star(\tau, \rho_{\max})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tau}}I$. Moreover, the following assertions hold. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item if $\widehat\lambda_i < \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tau}}$, then $\widehat\lambda_i < \lambda_i(\Sigma^\star(\tau,\rho))$ for any $\rho\in (0,\rho_{\max}]$,
        \item if $\widehat\lambda_i > \sqrt{\frac{1}{\tau}}$, then $\widehat\lambda_i > \lambda_i(\Sigma^\star(\tau,\rho))$ for any $\rho\in (0, \rho_{\max}]$,
        \item $\kappa(\Sigma^\star(\tau, \rho)) < \kappa(\widehat\Sigma)$ for any $\rho\in(0, \rho_{\max}]$, and $\kappa(\Sigma^\star(\tau, \rho))$ is strictly decreasing on $ \rho$.
    \end{enumerate}

\label{prop:consistency}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:unbounded}
nodes.statement: Let widehatSigma = Q^top Lambda Q be the spectral decomposition of widehatSigma with lambda_1geqldotsgeqlambda_r>lambda_r+1=ldots=lambda_p=0 being eigenvalues of widehatSigma. Let Sigma_eta = widehatSigma + eta I and X_eta=Sigma_eta^-1 for eta>0. Then (Sigma_eta, X_eta) is a feasible solution. The objective function at the feasible point (Sigma_eta, X_eta) can be evaluated by &-logdet (widehatSigma + eta I)^-1 + langle (widehatSigma + eta I)^-1,widehatSigmarangle +frac12tau \|eta I\|_F^2 - frac12tau \|widehatSigma\|_F^2\\ \;=\; &sum_i=1^p log (lambda_i+eta) + Trleft(Q^top Lambda Q (Q^top(Lambda+eta I)Q)^-1right) + frac12tau eta p - frac12tau \|widehatSigma\|_F^2\\ \;=\; &sum_i=1^r log (lambda_i+eta) + sum_i=r+1^p log eta + Trleft(Lambda(Lambda+eta I)^-1right) + frac12tau eta p- frac12tau \|widehatSigma\|_F^2\\\;=\; &sum_i=1^r log (lambda_i+eta) + sum_i=r+1^p log eta + sum_i=1^r fraclambda_ilambda_i+eta+ frac12tau eta p- frac12tau \|widehatSigma\|_F^2. The function value goes to -infty as etadownarrow 0.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $\widehat\Sigma = Q^\top \Lambda Q$ be the spectral decomposition of $\widehat\Sigma$ with 
$\lambda_1\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_r>\lambda_{r+1}=\ldots=\lambda_p=0$ being eigenvalues of $\widehat\Sigma$. Let $\Sigma_\eta = \widehat\Sigma + \eta I$ 
and $X_\eta=\Sigma_\eta^{-1}$ for $\eta>0$.  Then $(\Sigma_\eta, X_\eta)$ is a feasible solution. The objective function at the feasible point $(\Sigma_\eta, X_\eta)$ can be evaluated by
\begin{align*}
    &-\log\det (\widehat\Sigma + \eta I)^{-1} + \langle (\widehat\Sigma + \eta I)^{-1},\widehat{\Sigma}\rangle +\frac{1}{2}\tau \|\eta I\|_F^2 - \frac{1}{2}\tau \|\widehat\Sigma\|_F^2\\ \;=\; &\sum_{i=1}^p \log (\lambda_i+\eta) + \mathrm{Tr}\left(Q^\top \Lambda Q (Q^\top(\Lambda+\eta I)Q)^{-1}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\tau \eta p - \frac{1}{2}\tau \|\widehat\Sigma\|_F^2\\ \;=\; &\sum_{i=1}^r \log (\lambda_i+\eta) + \sum_{i=r+1}^p \log \eta + \mathrm{Tr}\left(\Lambda(\Lambda+\eta I)^{-1}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\tau \eta p- \frac{1}{2}\tau \|\widehat\Sigma\|_F^2\\\;=\; &\sum_{i=1}^r \log (\lambda_i+\eta) + \sum_{i=r+1}^p \log \eta + \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i+\eta}+ \frac{1}{2}\tau \eta p- \frac{1}{2}\tau \|\widehat\Sigma\|_F^2.
\end{align*}
The function value goes to $-\infty$ as $\eta\downarrow 0$.

    If Assumptions~\ref{ass:regularity-nominal}-\ref{ass:Spectral-divergence} hold, then the following assertions hold.

        \item The feasible set of~\eqref{prob:P-Mat} is compact if and only if the feasible set of~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow} is compact.
        \item If $s^\star$ is an optimal solution to~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow}, then $\widehat V\mathrm{diag}(s^\star){\widehat V}^\top$ is an optimal solution to~\eqref{prob:P-Mat}.
        \item If $\Sigma^\star$ is an optimal solution to~\eqref{prob:P-Mat}, then $\lambda(\Sigma^\star)$ is an optimal solution to~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow}. 
        \item The optimal values of~\eqref{prob:P-Mat} and~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow} are equal.
    \end{enumerate}

We proceed with the proof in two steps.

    \textbf{Step 1}. We show that problem~\eqref{prob:vector} admits a unique optimal solution. To this end, we show that the feasible set 
    $$
    \mathcal{S}\triangleq\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p_+:\sum_{i=1}^p d(s_i,\widehat\lambda_i)\leq  \rho\}
    $$ 
    is convex and compact and the objective is strictly convex over the set. Convexity of the set is implied by the convexity of $d$. To show compactness, it suffices to show closeness and boundedness of the set. The former is guaranteed by the continuity of $d$ under Assumption~\ref{ass:Spectral-divergence}~(ii). To show the boundedness, we note that by Remark~\ref{remark:minimizer-of-b}, $d(s_i,\widehat\lambda_i) = D(s_i I, \widehat\lambda_i I) / p$. Consequently, the feasible set can be written as $$
    \mathcal{S}=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p_+:\sum_{i=1}^p D(s_i I, \widehat\lambda_i I) / p\leq  \rho\}.
    $$
    Since $p>1$, then 
    $$
    S\subset \{s_i\in\mathbb{R}_+: D(s_i I,\widehat\lambda_i I)\leq  \rho\}.
    $$
    Assumption~\ref{ass:convex-divergence} (iii) ensures that the latter is bounded, which implies that $\mathcal{S}$ is bounded as desired. Since the objective function is continuous and strictly convex over the feasible set, the existence of a unique optimal solution is evident. 

    \textbf{Step 2}. Let $s^\star$ be the optimal solution to problem~\eqref{prob:vector}.
    We show that $s^\star={s^\star}^{\uparrow}$, and thus $s^\star$ is also optimal to~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow}. Let $q(s)\triangleq \sum_{i=1}^p \log s_i - \tau \sum_{i=1}^p s_i^2$ be the objective function of~\eqref{prob:vector}. Assume for the sake of a contradiction that $s^\star\neq {s^\star}^\uparrow$. Then by the feasibility of $s^\star$ and Lemma~\ref{lemma:rearrangement-ineq}, 
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{i=1}^p d({{s_i^\star}^\uparrow}, \widehat{\lambda}_i)<  \sum_{i=1}^p d({{s_i^\star}}, \widehat{\lambda}_i)\leq   \rho,
    \end{equation}
    which means ${s^\star}^\uparrow$ is feasible to~\eqref{prob:vector}. Moreover, $q(s^\star)=q({s^\star}^\uparrow)$, which means ${s^\star}^\uparrow$ is also optimal to~\eqref{prob:vector}. This is a contradiction to the fact that $s^\star$ is the unique optimal solution. Finally, we note that the feasible set of~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow} is a subset of that of~\eqref{prob:vector}, and thus $s^\star$ is the unique optimal solution to~\eqref{prob:vector-uparrow}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:consistency}
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to~citet[Proposition 7]ref:yue2024geometric. In this proof, we write x^star_i,n=lambda_i(Sigma^star_n(tau, rho_n)) and widehatx_i,n=lambda_i(widehatSigma) for i=1,ldots,n and nin N. By the strong consistency assumption, widehatSigma_n converges to Sigma_0 almost surely as ntoinfty. Now fix a particular realization of the uncertainties, where widehatSigma_n converges to Sigma_0 deterministically. Then it holds that lim_ntoinfty widehatx_i,n=lambda_i(Sigma_0) for i=1,ldots,p since the eigenvalue mapping lambda_i is continuous. On the other hand, by Proposition~(ii) we know that 0leq x^star_i,n leq maxleft\sqrtfrac1tau,bright\, i.e., \x^star_i,n\_ninN is bounded. Let \x^star_i,n_k\_kinN be a convergent subsequence of \x^star_i,n\_ninN. Then by Assumption~, it holds that dleft(x^star_i,n_k,widehatx_i,n_kright) leq sum_j=1^p d(x^star_j,n_k,widehatx_j,n_k) = Dleft(Sigma^star_n(tau, rho_n), widehatSigma_nright) leq rho_n_k, forall k inN, for i=1,ldots,p. Since rho_n_k converges to 0 and d is continuous by Assumption~ (ii), then implies that dleft(lim_ktoinfty x^star_i,n_k,lambda_i(Sigma_0)right) = dleft(lim_ktoinfty x^star_i,n_k,lim_ktoinfty widehatx_i,n_kright) = lim_ktoinftydleft(x^star_i,n_k,widehatx_i,n_kright) = 0. Recall that by Assumption~, d satisfies the identity of indiscernibles. Thus implies that lim_ktoinfty x^star_i,n_k=lambda_i(Sigma_0). This shows that every convergent subsequence of the bounded sequence \x^star_i,n\_ninN must have the same limit lambda_i(Sigma_0). By, it holds that lim_ntoinfty x^star_i,n = lambda_i(Sigma_0). The derivation so far applies to every uncertainty realization where widehatSigma_n converges to Sigma_0 deterministically. Since widehatSigma_n converges to Sigma_0 almost surely, we conclude that x^star_i,n converges to lambda_i(Sigma_0) almost surely. This implies that Pleft(lim_ntoinfty \|Sigma_n^star(tau, rho_n)-Sigma_0\|_F=0right) \;geq\; &Pleft(lim_ntoinftyleft( \|Sigma_n^star(tau, rho_n)-widehatSigma_n\|_F+\|widehatSigma_n-Sigma_0\|_Fright)=0right)\\ \;=\; &Pleft(lim_ntoinftyleft(\|x_n^star-widehatx_n\|_2+\|widehatSigma_n-Sigma_0\|_Fright)=0right)\\ \;geq \;&Pleft(lim_ntoinftyleft(\|x_n^star-lambda(Sigma_0)\|_2+\|widehatx_n-lambda(Sigma_0)\|_2+\|widehatSigma_n-Sigma_0\|_Fright)=0right) \\ \;= \; &1, where x_n^star and widehatx_n are the vectors of x^star_i,n,i=1,ldots,p and widehatx_i,n,i=1,ldots,p, and lambda(Sigma_0) is the eigenvalue vector of Sigma_0. Both inequalities hold because of the triangle inequality. The first equality holds by the fact that \|Sigma_n^star(tau, rho_n)-widehatSigma_n\|_F=\|x_n^star-widehatx_n\|_2 since Sigma_n^star(tau, rho_n) and widehatSigma_n share the same eigenvectors. The last equality holds by the fact that x^star_n converges to lambda(Sigma_0) almost surely, widehatx_n converges to lambda(Sigma_0) almost surely, and widehatSigma_n converges to Sigma_0 almost surely. This shows that Sigma^star_n(tau, rho_n) converges to Sigma_0 almost surely and completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:rate-of-d}
nodes.statement: Recall that F_lambda(gamma) = sum_i=1^p d(varphi(tau, gamma, lambda_i), lambda_i). It suffices to prove that lim_gammato infty gamma^2 d(varphi(tau, gamma, b), b) = C_b,d left(frac1/b-tau bd_b^primeprime(b) right)^2 for any fixed tau >0 and b>0. Let f(a) = frac1a-tau a -gamma d_b^prime(a). Recall that varphi(tau, gamma, b) is defined as the unique positive solution of f(a)=0. By Taylor expansion of f at point b to the first order, we obtain f(a) = frac1b - tau b + left(-frac1b^2-tau -gamma d_b^primeprime(b)right)(a-b) + o(|a-b|). Let varphi_tau,b(gamma) triangleq varphi(tau, gamma, b), and set f(varphi_tau,b(gamma))=0, i.e., varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b = frac1/b-tau b1/b^2+tau+gamma d_b^primeprime(b) + o(|varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b|). Then (varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b)^2 = \;&left[frac1/b-tau b1/b^2+tau+gamma d_b^primeprime(b)right]^2 + o(|varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b|^2). Consequently lim_gammatoinfty gamma^2 (varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b)^2 =lim_gamma to inftyleft[frac1/b-tau b1/gamma b^2+tau/gamma+d_b^primeprime(b)right]^2 = left(frac1/b-tau bd_b^primeprime(b)right)^2. Together with Assumption~, we have \[ lim_gamma to infty gamma^2 d(varphi(tau, gamma, b), b) = lim_gamma to infty fracd(varphi(tau, gamma, b), b)(varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b)^2 cdot gamma^2 (varphi_tau,b(gamma)-b)^2 = C_b,d left(frac1/b-tau bd_b^primeprime(b)right)^2. \] The proof is complete.

Recall that $F_{\lambda}(\gamma) = \sum_{i=1}^p d(\varphi(\tau, \gamma, \lambda_i), \lambda_i)$.
    It suffices to prove that 
    \begin{eqnarray} 
        \lim_{\gamma\to \infty} \gamma^2 d(\varphi(\tau, \gamma, b), b) = C_{b,d} \left(\frac{1/b-\tau b}{d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)} \right)^2
    \end{eqnarray} 
    for any fixed $\tau >0$ and $b>0$.
    Let 
    $
        f(a) = \frac{1}{a}-\tau a -\gamma d_b^\prime(a).
    $
    Recall that $\varphi(\tau, \gamma, b)$ is defined as the unique positive solution of $f(a)=0$.
 By Taylor expansion of $f$ at point $b$ to the first order, we obtain
    \begin{align*}
        f(a) = \frac{1}{b} - \tau b + \left(-\frac{1}{b^2}-\tau -\gamma d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)\right)(a-b) + o(|a-b|).
    \end{align*}
    Let $\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma) \triangleq \varphi(\tau, \gamma, b)$, and set $f(\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma))=0$, i.e., 
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b = \frac{1/b-\tau b}{1/b^2+\tau+\gamma d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)} + o(|\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b|).
    \end{align*}
    Then 
    \begin{align*}
        (\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b)^2 = 
         \;&\left[\frac{1/b-\tau b}{1/b^2+\tau+\gamma d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)}\right]^2 + o(|\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b|^2).
    \end{align*}
    Consequently
    \begin{align*}
        \lim_{\gamma\to\infty} \gamma^2 (\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b)^2 =\lim_{\gamma \to \infty}\left[\frac{1/b-\tau b}{1/\gamma b^2+\tau/\gamma+d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)}\right]^2 = \left(\frac{1/b-\tau b}{d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)}\right)^2.
    \end{align*}
    Together with Assumption~\ref{ass:like-frob}, we have 
    \[
        \lim_{\gamma \to \infty} \gamma^2 d(\varphi(\tau, \gamma, b), b) = 
        \lim_{\gamma \to \infty}  
        \frac{d(\varphi(\tau, \gamma, b), b)}{(\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b)^2 } \cdot \gamma^2 (\varphi_{\tau,b}(\gamma)-b)^2
        =
        C_{b,d} \left(\frac{1/b-\tau b}{d_b^{\prime\prime}(b)}\right)^2.
    \]
    The proof is complete.

Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ be eigenvalues of $\Sigma_0$. Then, it suffices to prove
    \begin{eqnarray} 
        \sum_{i=1}^p \frac{1}{\lambda_i} \geq \frac{p}{\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i^2}\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i.
    \end{eqnarray}

 $
        \sum_{i=1}^p \frac{1}{\lambda_i} \geq \frac{p^2}{\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i},
    $
    where the inequality becomes equality if and only if all the eigenvalues are identical, i.e., $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\ldots=\lambda_p$.

    \begin{align*}
        \left(\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i\cdot 1\right)^2 \leq p\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{p}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i\right)^2} \geq \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i^2}\;\Rightarrow\; \frac{p^2}{\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i} \geq \frac{p}{\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i\right),
    \end{align*}
    where the inequalities become equalities if and only if $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\ldots=\lambda_p$.
